headline: Lawsuit alleges Grok used to create 7,000 CSAM images of stepdaughter; X accused of obstruction
summary: An expanded class action lawsuit accuses X and xAI of creating "toxic AI nudify tools" and obstructing police investigations into Grok-generated child sex abuse material.
details: An expanded class action lawsuit now accuses X and xAI of building "toxic AI nudify tools" and shielding child predators. The suit alleges they obstructed police investigations into Grok-generated child sex abuse materials (CSAM).

In one horrific case, a stepfather allegedly used Grok to create 7,000 sexually explicit images of his stepdaughter, taken when she was 11. He later took his own life after police discovered the images.

The complaint states Grok allowed the generation of extreme images, including incest and rape, without flagging harmful behavior. xAI's safety system reportedly only intervened after a "gang rape" prompt, triggering a CyberTip to NCMEC.

Despite mandatory reporting requirements, xAI allegedly refused to help law enforcement or NCMEC identify the user for weeks. This obstruction made it harder for police to locate and apprehend the perpetrator.

The stepfather was eventually arrested after a warrant seized his devices, revealing approximately 7,000 AI-generated images. His family believes he would not have created these images without Grok's "undressing" capabilities.
The lawsuit details the profound impact on Jane Doe 4, who now suffers from anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts. Her family was torn apart by the dual tragedies of exploitation and suicide.

Legal teams highlight that NCMEC found 90% of xAI's CyberTipline reports in early 2026 were unactionable due to missing user information. xAI allegedly omitted critical data like IP addresses, stymying investigations.

Jane Doe 4 accused X of going "silent" after Grok transformed a photo of her as a child into thousands of explicit images. She stated, "This technology is a free, easily accessible weapon put into the hands of the worst people in the world."
Another plaintiff, Jane Doe 5, was also targeted by an acquaintance who trafficked alleged Grok-generated images online. She was only notified after the perpetrator's arrest.

headline_marked: [[ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok tested]] on real coding bugs: No single 'best AI' winner found
headline: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok tested on real coding bugs: No single 'best AI' winner found
summary: A new comparison put top AI models like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok against real-world coding tasks, revealing that the 'best' AI varies significantly by the specific job, from debugging to greenfield development.
details: A recent, rigorous comparison tested leading AI models—ChatGPT (GPT-5.2), Claude (Opus 4.8), Gemini (3.1 Pro), and Grok 4—side-by-side on actual coding tasks. This wasn't a benchmark, but a practical assessment of their performance on 'I need this to work by Friday' scenarios.

The most significant finding was that there was no single 'best AI for coding.' The top performer changed depending on the specific task, indicating that each model has distinct strengths and weaknesses.

For tackling gnarly bugs in existing code, reasoning-heavy models like Claude Opus and GPT-5.2 proved superior. They were able to identify subtle errors, such as off-by-one or stale-closure bugs, that faster models often missed or confidently provided incorrect solutions for.

When it came to greenfield development, like scaffolding a small service from requirements, all models demonstrated competence. The differences were more about stylistic preferences—some over-engineered, while others delivered lean, readable code.

In tasks requiring comprehension, such as explaining complex legacy code, models that remained literal and avoided 'improving' the code performed best. Those that tried to refactor while explaining were often less helpful.

The gap was most brutal for obscure libraries or very recent APIs. Models with live web access or fresher knowledge cutoffs provided accurate answers, while others often hallucinated confident but incorrect method signatures, leading to wasted development time.

Watching four AI answers simultaneously highlighted a critical insight: wrong answers are delivered with the same confidence as correct ones. Disagreements between models serve as a crucial signal, prompting developers to think critically rather than blindly trusting a single AI.

The takeaway is that relying on just one coding AI is limiting. A multi-model approach, allowing developers to compare outputs and identify discrepancies, is recommended for a more robust and efficient workflow.
